opening.headline: To prevent deployments from failing immediately after an upgrade, the upgrade schedule must be incorporated into the plan, including Kubernetes release cycles, support lifecycles, and API deprecation timelines.
body: After upgrading the cluster to a new minor version, the deployment pipeline immediately fails because the manifest's apiVersion is no longer supported by the new API server. Upgrades are infrastructure operations as well as deployment compatibility operations.

In this lesson, we will sequentially examine which Kubernetes versions are supported for how long, how to read end-of-support dates from the release schedule, the process by which APIs are phased out, and the order in which upgrades are performed. Finally, we will illustrate a practical example of planning for a scenario where only three months remain until end-of-support.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the Kubernetes release cycle and support lifecycle.
You can distinguish the impact of support schedules and API discontinuation on change plans.

screens.title: Deployment failed after upgrade
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare how the same manifest differs before and after the upgrade.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing a previously successful deployment failing due to API version errors after an upgrade.
labels: This apiVersion is no longer provided.

states.label: Before upgrade
states.body: This is running on a previous minor version that supports clusters, and the deployment pipeline succeeds every day. The repository still contains the old manifests written long ago. For example, it includes the PodDisruptionBudget for `policy/v1beta1` and the FlowSchema for `flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1beta3`. Since these API versions are still available, no issues are apparent. That is precisely why older apiVersion are quietly accumulating.

states.label: After upgrade
states.body: Immediately after upgrading the cluster to a new minor version, the deployment pipeline fails. The cause is that the manifest was using an API version that is no longer available in the new version. PodDisruptionBudget in `policy/v1beta1` is no longer available starting from v1.25, and `flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1beta3` is no longer available starting from v1.32. Upgrades are not only infrastructure team responsibilities but also compatibility tasks that affect all deployment manifests. This course covers methods for proactively preventing such issues.

screens.outro: Let us recall how well our cluster is prepared for this issue.

screens.title: Does our cluster have a version policy?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are organized and revealed. Since there are no items to input or submit, first recall your own cluster.

items.prompt: What is the currently running Kubernetes minor version?
items.answer: The version is denoted as x.y.z, where x represents major, y represents minor, and z represents patch. The support period and the basic unit of API changes are based on minor versions, so knowing the first two digits, such as 1.35, serves as the starting point.

items.prompt: When will this version receive patches?
items.answer: Each minor version has a scheduled end-of-support date listed in the timetable. If it's not possible to provide an exact answer, it means that this information has not yet been included in any planned changes. In this course, you will learn how to read the timetable.

items.prompt: Is there not an outdated apiVersion remaining in the manifest?
items.answer: Distribution files are rarely modified after being created, making beta versions tend to persist for a long time. If not moved before an upgrade, they will be revealed on the day of the upgrade.

screens.outro: First, let's examine how release cycles and support lifespans are determined.

screens.title: Release Cycle and Support Lifespan
screens.lead: The following table contains part of the release schedule. Check what each column represents and compare the end-of-support dates by minor version.

visual.alt: A timeline diagram showing the support period for four minor releases.

data.caption: Support Schedule by Minor Release
data.notes: The Kubernetes project maintains release branches for the most recent three minor releases. Versions after 1.19 receive patch support for approximately one year, while versions prior to 1.18 receive support for about nine months. Releases that have ended support no longer receive security updates or bug fixes. Patch releases occur regularly and have pre-defined cherry-pick deadlines, allowing for predictable scheduling of which fixes will be included in a given patch. The dates in the table are all scheduled values, and support periods vary by minor version, resulting in sequential end-of-support dates. First, verify which row in the table corresponds to your currently running version. The project recommends upgrading to the latest patch as quickly as possible to remain on a supported minor version.

screens.outro: The support timeline is constrained by time; now we will look at content constraints, specifically API removal.

screens.title: How to Read About API Sunset and Removal
screens.lead: When you select an item to expand, you can see which APIs are no longer provided by release and what alternatives are available.

items.title: The API is removed after being deprecated
items.body: The Kubernetes API evolves over time. Older versions first become deprecated and, starting from a specific release, the API server no longer provides those versions. This is referred to as "stopped serving." The removal release table shows which features are removed in which version and the target versions to which they are migrated.

items.title: v1.22: Webhook Setup and CRD
items.body: The MutatingWebhookConfiguration and ValidatingWebhookConfiguration for API group `admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1beta1` are no longer available and must be migrated to `admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1`. After migration, default values change: the default value for `webhooks[*].failurePolicy` changes from `Ignore` to `Fail`, and `timeoutSeconds` changes from 30 seconds to 10 seconds. Even if fields with the same name are left unchanged, the behavior may differ.

items.title: v1.25: PodSecurityPolicy, PDB, HPA, CronJob
items.body: In v1.25, several APIs were consolidated. The PodSecurityPolicy from `policy/v1beta1` is retired, and the admission controller is removed, so it is migrated to Pod Security Admission or third-party admission webhooks. PodDisruptionBudget is moved to `policy/v1`, HorizontalPodAutoscaler to `autoscaling/v2`, and CronJob to `batch/v1`. The meaning of the empty PodDisruptionBudget from `spec.selector` has changed in v1, such that it now selects all pods in the namespace.

items.title: v1.26, v1.29, v1.32: HPA and flow control
items.body: In v1.26, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler for `autoscaling/v2beta2` was removed, along with FlowSchema and PriorityLevelConfiguration from `flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1beta1`. In v1.29, `v1beta2` was removed and moved to `flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1`; in v1.32, `v1beta3` was removed and moved to `flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1`. Occasionally, an API group is gradually phased out over multiple releases.

items.title: What should be moved directly?
items.body: Previously stored objects can also be read using the new API. However, the manifest and API client must be moved directly. The documentation outlines three methods: provide `--runtime-config=<group>/<version>=false` to the API server to pre-simulate removal, find deprecated API usages through client warnings, metrics, and audit information, and update the YAML to use the new apiVersion. While conversion is possible using `kubectl convert -f <file> --output-version <group>/<version>`, the command may not have optimal defaults, so the results must be reviewed.

screens.outro: Now we'll consider both schedule and compatibility to determine the upgrade sequence.

screens.title: Combination of upgrade sequence and support schedule
screens.lead: Follow the step-by-step upgrade flow for a cluster created with kubeadm. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: An upgrade order that first upgrades control plane nodes, then worker nodes.
labels: From minor version 1.x to 1.x+1, no skipping allowed
Check release notes and backup app status

steps.title: Preparation: Release notes and backup
steps.body: Before upgrading, carefully read the release notes and backup important app-level state stored in the database. While `kubeadm upgrade` only handles Kubernetes internal components without touching the workload, backup is always a good practice.

steps.title: First control plane node
steps.body: The overall flow is first the control plane node, then the remaining control plane nodes, and finally the worker nodes. When upgrading the kubelet to a minor version, you must first drain the corresponding node. This is because control plane nodes may host important pods such as CoreDNS.

steps.title: The remaining control plane and worker nodes
steps.body: After upgrading the control plane, deploy the worker nodes. After the upgrade, the container specification hash values change, causing all containers to be restarted. It is recommended to match the kubelet and kubeadm versions; however, within supported ranges, the kubelet can be run at a lower version.

steps.title: Minor versions are not skipped.
steps.body: A kubeadm cluster can be upgraded by one minor version, or to a later patch within the same minor version. Skipping minor versions is unsupported. If you are two minor versions behind, you must upgrade one step at a time in two separate upgrades, doubling the work involved.

steps.title: Support end date has reached the deadline
steps.body: The project is advised to quickly apply the latest patch to maintain minor versions. Since minor versions must be incremented step by step, the upgrade start date should be determined by working backward from the end-of-support date. Therefore, the end-of-support date serves as the deadline for the change plan.

screens.outro: Let's apply the content we reviewed earlier to a real-world example.

screens.title: Explanation: A case of planning an upgrade three months before support end date
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: Upgrade plan timeline calculated backwards from end of support.

steps.title: sorting out the situation
steps.body: The current minor version is nearing end-of-support in five months and is two levels behind the latest version currently supported. In this situation, the team feels they should accelerate the upgrade, but rushing and planning are two different things.

steps.title: Step 1: Reverse calculate the schedule
steps.body: Since minor versions cannot be skipped, two upgrades are required. Calculate the date when two upgrades must be completed by counting backward from the end-of-support date, determine the duration required for each upgrade, and establish the preparation period prior to each upgrade. The three-month period must include all necessary buffer time for pre-validation and rollback.

steps.title: Step 2: Investigate the impact
steps.body: Compare the removal release list with the manifest to first identify the API version. During the two-step process, all releases between the two steps are targeted. Also refer to client warnings, metrics, and audit information; if necessary, retrieve the older version from the API server for pre-validation.

steps.title: Step 3: Move the manifest before upgrading
steps.body: First, upgrade to the new apiVersion to ensure deployment compatibility. The new version may have different default values, so review these values. For example, an empty selector in PodDisruptionBudget has a different meaning. Moving this configuration before upgrading the cluster prevents deployments from failing on the upgrade day.

steps.title: Step 4: Execute sequentially.
steps.body: After reading the release notes and completing a backup, first deploy the control plane and then deploy the worker nodes. Repeat this process in increments of two. Between each stage, drain the nodes and schedule the timing to account for the time it takes for all containers to restart after the upgrade.

steps.title: result
steps.body: You reach a supported version prior to end-of-support, and no deployment discontinuation has occurred. The support schedule is the deadline of the change plan, and the API removal list is the first task list of that plan.

screens.outro: Based on the example, I will summarize the key points.

screens.title: Align support schedule with API retirement as a single plan
screens.lead: This course covers release cycles, support lifespans, API removal, and upgrade sequences—summarized into a single workflow.

paragraphs: Kubernetes maintains the most recent three minor releases and provides patch support for minor versions approximately one year after the release of 1.19. A schedule is established for each minor version, specifying the start date of maintenance mode and the end date of support. After support ends, no security updates or bug fixes are provided. This date serves as the deadline for any change plans.

API goes through a deprecated phase and is discontinued starting from a specific release. Existing objects are readable using the new API, but requests sent to the removed version fail. The manifest and client must be manually migrated, and items with changed default values require separate review.

Upgrades skip minor versions and first upgrade the control plane before upgrading the worker nodes. Therefore, the schedule is calculated backward from the target date, and manifest prior to the cluster upgrade comes first.

Ultimately, the support timeline is constrained by time, while API removal is constrained by content. Only by considering both factors and establishing the correct order can we prevent the release from being disrupted on the day of the upgrade.

Going back to the initial scene, what the team lacked after the upgrade was not technology, but planning. If they had known their support end dates and cross-referenced their removal lists with their manifests, the same upgrade would have concluded as a scheduled task.

callout.label: organizing
callout.text: The support schedule is the deadline for the change plan.

glossary.def: This is the release corresponding to y in x.y.z. It is the basic unit for tracking support periods and API changes.
This minor release is the last day it will receive patches and security updates.
This is the process of initially not recommending the old API version and eventually discontinuing its provision starting from a specific release.
This is a support phase available for a specified period before support ends, with a start date scheduled in the timetable.
Rules regarding version differences allowed among cluster components.

misconceptions.myth: Minor versions can be skipped forward by one or more.
misconceptions.fact: Upgrading over minor versions is not supported. You must upgrade one step at a time, and the more behind you are, the more upgrade cycles will be required.

misconceptions.myth: When running kubeadm upgrade, the workload manifests also change to the new API.
misconceptions.fact: kubeadm upgrade focuses solely on internal Kubernetes components without touching workloads. Upgrading the manifest and client's apiVersion must be done manually.

misconceptions.myth: Since there are stored objects, the existing API version manifest can still be used.
misconceptions.fact: Stored objects can be read using the new API, but requests sent using the removed apiVersion fail.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The support schedule is the deadline for the change plan.
Recent minor releases are being maintained, and minor versions after 1.19 receive patches for approximately one year.
API support discontinuation means that support ends for a specific release, so the manifest must be moved in advance.
Upgrades first elevate the control plane, skipping no minor versions.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for you to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: When will support for our cluster end, and how many minor updates must we complete prior to that date?

checks.q: What is the most direct issue when operating a discontinued Kubernetes minor release?
options: No longer receiving security updates or bug fixes
The cluster immediately stops without receiving a new request.
The apiVersion of the existing manifest is automatically updated.
Stored objects are no longer readable via the new API.
checks.explain: Releases that have ended support do not receive security updates or bug fixes. Therefore, the support end date becomes the deadline for the change plan.

wrong.1: Support end does not necessarily mean cluster termination.
wrong.2: apiVersion does not change automatically and the manifest must be moved manually.
wrong.3: Saved objects are read via the new API, and only the manifest and client need to be moved directly.

checks.intro: This question asks about the impact of continuing to operate a release that has ended support. Please consider it in relation to your schedule table. The results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The most direct issue is that security updates will be discontinued after support ends.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again about what specifically support termination stops.

checks.q: Try the upgrade order for a kubeadm cluster.
items: Upgrade of remaining control plane nodes
checks.explain: Deploy the control plane first, then the worker nodes. Incremental upgrades are performed one step at a time without skipping minor versions.
checks.intro: This question demonstrates the order of kubeadm upgrades. Recall the steps you just followed. The results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: The sequence was accurately followed. Control plane comes first.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Please reconsider whether you are deploying the control plane or the worker node first.

checks.q: Before support ends, two minors must be released. What should be done first to prevent deployment interruption before the upgrade?
options: Upgrade all at once from the worker node to the latest minor version
Skip minor upgrades to reduce the number of stages.
Compare the removal release table and migrate the API version manifest to a new version.
Since the stored object is automatically converted, the manifest remains unchanged.
checks.explain: APIs removed are no longer available starting from that release, so you must locate the old apiVersion before upgrading and migrate to the new version to avoid deployment failures.

wrong.0: Deploying worker nodes first violates the recommended order and does not resolve API issues.
wrong.1: Skipping minor steps is not supported; steps must be incremented one at a time.
wrong.3: Stored objects are readable, but the manifest and client must be moved directly.

checks.intro: This question asks you to choose what to do first as the end-of-support approaches. Recall the order of case walkthroughs. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, the first step is to locate and move the removed apiVersion.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This is not something that needs to be done before an upgrade. Review once again the cause of the incident.
